core.big_idea: The flood story holds together divine judgment, preservation, and covenant promise.

passages.reading_note: Read the corruption, judgment announcement, and ark instructions.
Read the post-flood worship and covenant sign.

core.metanarrative_position: Judgment, preservation, and covenant: God responds to pervasive violence, preserves life, and binds the future with a promise.
core.biblical_genre: Primeval biblical narrative with covenant speech

claims.statement: Genesis attributes the flood judgment to pervasive human wickedness and violence.
God provides the ark as the means by which Noah’s household and animal life are preserved.
After the flood, God establishes a covenant with Noah, his descendants, and every living creature.
The rainbow is named as the sign of that covenant.
The story holds together judgment and mercy but does not authorize explaining each later disaster as direct punishment for its victims.
claims.prohibited_overstatement: Do not use the flood to claim that a modern disaster identifies its victims as more sinful than others.

core.interpretation_skill: Read the narrative in three lenses-judgment, preservation, covenant-and distinguish ancient narrative from modern disaster explanation.

learning.foundation_objective: Explain that the flood narrative includes judgment on violence, preservation through the ark, and a covenant promise, and place it on the timeline.
learning.extension_objective: Analyse the covenant recipients and sign, then state what the passage does and does not permit us to claim about later disasters.
know: Genesis links the flood to violence and corruption.
The ark preserves human and animal life.
The covenant includes Noah, descendants, and living creatures.
understand: Covenant is a binding promise initiated by God.
Judgment and mercy are not opposites in the narrative; both are present.
practise: Reject violence rather than normalise it.
Treat creation as belonging within God’s covenant concern.
become: A student who reads difficult judgment narratives carefully and responds with humility rather than accusation.
success_evidence: The student fills all three lenses with textual evidence.
The student identifies the covenant recipients and sign.
The student rejects simplistic disaster blame.

zero_prep_card.objective: Students explain the flood through judgment, preservation, and covenant promise.
zero_prep_card.opening: Write Judgment, Preservation, and Promise. Ask whether one story can contain all three.
say: Genesis describes a world filled with corruption and violence.
God announces judgment and provides an ark that preserves life.
After the flood, God makes a covenant with Noah, future descendants, and living creatures.
The rainbow is a sign of God’s covenant, not a charm that prevents every disaster.
ask: What reason for judgment does Genesis give?
What claim about modern disasters would go beyond the text?
zero_prep_card.do: Complete the Three-Lens Flood Grid with direct evidence for judgment, preservation, and covenant.
zero_prep_card.close: Pray for humility before difficult texts, rejection of violence, and care for living things.

preparation.passage_context: Genesis 6-9 is an extended narrative framed by human violence, divine judgment, preservation, sacrifice, covenant, and renewed commission. This lesson does not attempt to resolve scientific flood models.
text_observations: “Violence” and “corrupt” are repeated in the judgment rationale.
The ark instructions repeatedly concern preservation and continuation of life.
The covenant explicitly includes future generations and every living creature.
interpretation_notes: Covenant should be defined as a binding promise or committed relationship, not merely a casual agreement.
Keep questions about flood extent and chronology separate from the passage’s theological claims unless deliberately researched later.
Use Luke 13 only as a canonical guardrail against victim-blaming; do not make it the primary passage.
theological_guardrails: Do not soften the judgment into a harmless animal story.
Do not use graphic descriptions or invite speculation about individual victims.
Do not claim every rainbow is a new covenant or a magical protective object.

likely_questions.question: Was the flood global?
likely_questions.purpose: Say Christians and scholars debate geographical and scientific models; this lesson focuses on the claims the narrative clearly makes.

likely_questions.question: Why would God judge so severely?
likely_questions.purpose: Return to the text’s portrayal of pervasive evil and violence, acknowledge the difficulty, and avoid pretending the emotional problem disappears.

discussion_questions.question: What words describe the world before the flood?
How does the ark function in the narrative?
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Distinguish God’s provision from Noah earning salvation.

discussion_questions.question: Who are the covenant partners and what is the sign?
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Discuss the ecological breadth of the covenant.

discussion_questions.question: Why is it wrong to call every disaster a direct punishment of its victims?
discussion_questions.foundation_prompt: The flood gives its own stated reason; later events need their own evidence.
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Use Luke 13 cautiously as a canonical check.

family.title: Three Lenses on the Flood
family.parent_intro: This study reads the flood as a serious account of violence, judgment, preservation, and promise.

flow.instructions: Use the opening prompt to connect the lesson to ordinary family life.
Find one detail for each heading: Judgment, Preservation, Covenant.
Draw three circles labelled Noah, Descendants, Living Creatures and place the rainbow sign around them.
Choose the weekly action, then pray together.

questions: What reason does Genesis give for judgment?
Who is included in the covenant?

interactive.title: Judgment-Preservation-Covenant
interactive.instructions: Place passage details under the three headings and identify the covenant sign.

family.weekly_action: Choose one action that protects life or reduces harm in your household or neighbourhood.
family.prayer: God, teach us to reject violence, receive mercy with gratitude, and care for life.
family.parent_note: Do not use a modern disaster or family tragedy as an example of direct divine punishment.

quiz.question: What condition does Genesis repeatedly name before the flood?
quiz.explanation: The narrative gives a moral rationale for judgment.

quiz.question: Who is included in the covenant?
quiz.explanation: Genesis 9 explicitly widens the covenant recipients.

quiz.question: The rainbow is named as the covenant sign.
quiz.explanation: Genesis 9 identifies the bow as the sign.

quiz.question: Which claim goes beyond the lesson’s evidence?
options: Every modern disaster proves its victims were worse sinners

answer.text: Every modern disaster proves its victims were worse sinners

quiz.explanation: The narrative does not authorize universal victim-blaming.

accessibility.reading_level: Upper-primary discussion with concrete anchors before abstract explanation.
accessibility.plain_language_rule: Define covenant, genre, inference, and other technical terms before expecting use.
neurodiversity_supports: Use a visible timeline or comparison grid.
Allow written, drawn, or spoken responses.
Model one completed example before independent work.
sensory_notes: Offer a seated alternative to movement activities.
non_reader_support: Use prepared cards so participation does not depend on fluent reading.

do_not_ask: Do not ask students to connect personal disasters with divine punishment.
Do not invite graphic descriptions of flood deaths or violence.
safeguarding.teacher_response: Acknowledge the narrative’s severity, use selected passages, and route personal grief questions privately and safely.
